title: The Lantern of the Palatinate
premise: In 1748 Heidelberg, Edmund Fairweather is a woman living as a man, apprenticed to the clockmaker father who forged her papers to keep her safe after her mother's exile. When census taker Margarethe Vogel notices the discrepancy between the guild rolls and the household, Edmund's careful invisibility begins to crack, forcing her father to reveal the truth about the mother who still lives across the sea in the Palatine diaspora. As the last emigrant ship prepares to sail and the observatory's master clock fails, Edmund must decide whether to stay in the identity her father built for her or claim her own name — and when only one berth remains, she gives it to her ailing father, sending him to the mother she has never known while she stays to keep the clock, and her own chosen life, running. The novel ends with Edmund signing her true name in the guild book, visible at last.
about_author: Ansel Fairweather is the pen name of a former horologist's apprentice who spent a decade restoring tower clocks in Rhineland churches before turning to fiction. Their work draws on family letters recovered from an eighteenth-century Palatine emigration, and on the quiet conviction that history is mostly kept by people no census bothered to name.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Edmund Fairweather's POV. Summoned to repair the Heidelberg observatory's failing master clock, Edmund is interrupted by census taker Margarethe Vogel, whose questions about the household's 'missing daughter' land too precisely. Edmund deflects, but her hands shake on the escapement. Beat: the first crack in twelve years of careful silence.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, moving between present and memory. Flashback to her mother's flight after the 1743 persecutions, her father's decision to apprentice 'his son,' and the rules she lives by: bind her chest, never sing, never weep in daylight. Beat: the cost of invisibility made intimate and specific.

chapters.title: The Guild Rolls
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. A dutiful clerk with her own secrets, Margarethe cross-checks the census against guild records and finds Edmund's apprenticeship paper dated three days after the daughter's recorded death. She tells herself it's only an error. Beat: curiosity hardening into obligation.

chapters.title: Oil and Iron
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Working nights on the master clock, Edmund finds her father Jakob's hidden ledger: payments, forged documents, and a sealed letter addressed to a name she doesn't recognize in Rotterdam. Beat: the discovery that her whole identity is a mechanism someone else built.

chapters.title: The Visitor at Vespers
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. Margarethe calls at the Fairweather workshop under pretense of follow-up questions and watches Edmund too closely; Jakob intervenes with practiced charm. Margarethe leaves unconvinced — and unsettled by her own sympathy. Beat: the hunter doubting the hunt.

chapters.title: What the Clock Keeps
chapters.summary: Jakob's POV. Jakob reflects on his bargain: he saved his child by erasing his daughter, and has never asked whether the trade was fair. He begins drafting a letter he cannot send. Beat: a father's guilt rendered through the language of gears and tolerances.

chapters.title: Rotterdam Letters
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund steams open the sealed letter and learns her mother Anna lives in a Palatine exile community in Pennsylvania, and that a ship — the last subsidized berth of the season — sails on the morning tide in six weeks. Beat: the abstract past becomes a person with an address.

chapters.title: The Census Book
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. Pressured by her magistrate superior to close the census cleanly, Margarethe must either file the discrepancy or investigate it. She delays, visiting the workshop again and finding Edmund singing, alone, thinking no one hears. Beat: the secret shared without a word.

chapters.title: An Agreement of Silences
chapters.summary: Edmund and Margarethe, alternating. Confronted, Edmund neither confirms nor denies; Margarethe offers a fragile truce — her silence in exchange for Edmund's story. Both recognize something of themselves in the other. Beat: alliance formed across an impossible divide.

chapters.title: The Master Clock Fails
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The observatory clock stops entirely, and the university threatens to give the contract to a rival guild — meaning exposure, inspection, and questions Edmund cannot survive. Beat: external stakes collapse onto the internal secret.

chapters.title: Jakob's Tremor
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Jakob's hands begin to shake — the fine work is slipping beyond him, and with it the fiction of the able master clockmaker. Edmund quietly completes his commissions, becoming the craftsman her papers say she is. Beat: the disguise becoming truth.

chapters.title: Margarethe's Own Ledger
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. Revealed: Margarethe's census role is penance imposed after her brother was transported for forgery; accuracy is her redemption. Filing Edmund means destroying someone the way the state once destroyed her family. Beat: the antagonist fully humanized.

chapters.title: The Rival's Eye
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Guild rival Konrad Brenner, sniffing advantage, hints to Margarethe's magistrate that the Fairweather papers are false. The truce strains as Margarethe must choose between her redemption and Edmund's life. Beat: rising tension, the noose tightening.

chapters.title: Anna's Voice
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A letter arrives from Rotterdam — forwarded through the exile network — in her mother's hand, addressed not to Jakob but to the daughter's true name. Edmund reads it aloud to an empty workshop and weeps for the first time in years. Beat: identity as inheritance, not erasure.

chapters.title: The Confession at the Clock
chapters.summary: Edmund and Jakob. On the observatory tower, Edmund tells her father she wants to sail — to meet Anna, to be herself somewhere new. Jakob, hiding the worsening tremor, agrees to apply for the berth as her father, never guessing what she is planning. Beat: love expressed as mutual deception.

chapters.title: Brenner's Report
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. Brenner files a formal accusation; the magistrate orders the Fairweather household inspected before the ship sails — in eleven days. Margarethe, holding the file, must decide what to do with the paper that could save or hang them. Beat: the climax set in motion.

chapters.title: What Margarethe Burned
chapters.summary: Margarethe's POV. Margarethe destroys the discrepancy report and forges a clean census entry, knowing it may cost her position and her brother's pardon petition. She delivers the forged page to Edmund with the words: 'Now you owe the truth to someone.' Beat: sacrifice and demand entwined.

chapters.title: The Last Berth
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The berth is granted — one only, and the ship sails on the morning tide. Edmund discovers Jakob has secretly listed himself, intending to send her to Anna while he faces the inspection alone. Beat: the central choice made flesh; both parent and child trying to give the future to the other.

chapters.title: The Night Wind
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, the novel's climax. Edmund finishes the master clock, sets it running true, and at dawn forces the choice: she puts her trembling father on the boat to the mother who can nurse him, and stays to answer the magistrate herself. On the dock, Jakob finally calls her by her true name. Beat: the berth given; the self claimed; farewell.

chapters.title: Before the Magistrate
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Standing inspection, Edmund speaks the truth plainly — her name, her work, the clock above them all keeping perfect time. Margarethe corroborates the guild papers' validity; Brenner's accusation collapses for lack of the census record. Beat: visibility chosen, at last, and survived.

chapters.title: The Guild Book
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund signs her true name in the guild roll as journeyman clockmaker — the first woman in the Heidelberg register — and takes over the observatory contract. Margarethe, dismissed but unbowed, asks to be taught to read a clock's works. Beat: belonging built rather than granted.

chapters.title: First Light on the Rhine
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, coda. A letter from Pennsylvania: Jakob restored, Anna's voice on the page, a promise of passage whenever Edmund chooses. She winds the master clock as the sun rises over the river and writes her reply, signing it with both names. Beat: resolution — inheritance reclaimed, identity whole, home chosen rather than assigned.
